title: The Life of Krishna
description: An illustrated map of Krishna’s life as tradition tells it, from the prison in Mathura and the cowherds’ Vrindavan to Dwaraka, Kurukshetra and Prabhasa, chapter by chapter.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the life of Krishna across India, from Mathura and Vrindavan to Dwaraka, Kurukshetra and Assam
note: Places follow traditional associations; where several places claim one, the cards name them. The story follows the Bhagavata Purana, with the Mahabharata for the epic chapters, and says where they differ. Mathura, Gokul, Vrindavan and Govardhan lie within about 30 kilometres of one another; here they are spread apart so each can be tapped, and a few other close places are nudged apart. Kingdom areas are loose regions. The map and the timeline are not to scale.

steps.title: A voice at the wedding
steps.text: Kamsa, prince of Mathura, drives the chariot at his cousin Devaki’s wedding to Vasudeva. A voice from the sky warns that her eighth child will kill him. He draws his sword on her; Vasudeva saves her by promising to hand over every child. Kamsa jails his father, King Ugrasena, takes the throne and kills Devaki’s first six sons.
steps.today: Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, on the Yamuna. A riverside fort called Kans Qila bears Kamsa’s name, though it was built in the 16th century.

steps.title: Born at midnight
steps.text: The seventh child, Balarama, is moved from Devaki’s womb to that of Rohini, another wife of Vasudeva, in Gokula. The eighth is born in the prison at midnight, appearing first as four-armed Vishnu, then as an ordinary baby. Tradition celebrates the night as Janmashtami, the eighth day of the waning moon in the monsoon month of Bhadrapada.
steps.today: Shri Krishna Janmasthan, Mathura, is honoured as the prison site. Some calendars name the month Shravana.

steps.title: Across the Yamuna
steps.text: The guards sleep and the gates open. Vasudeva carries the baby through a storm; the serpent Shesha spreads his hoods over them and the Yamuna lets them through. In Gokula he swaps the boy for the newborn daughter of Yashoda and Nanda. When Kamsa dashes her against a stone, she rises as a goddess and tells him his killer lives.
steps.today: Gokul and neighbouring Mahavan, across the Yamuna from Mathura, both claim Nanda’s home.

steps.title: Putana
steps.text: Kamsa sends demons to kill the newborns. Putana comes to Gokula as a beautiful woman and nurses the baby with poisoned milk; he sucks out her life with it, and her true, monstrous body crashes across the fields. Later he overturns a heavy cart with a kick, and a whirlwind demon (Trinavarta) who carries him into the sky is crushed.
steps.today: Gokul’s temples re-enact these stories for pilgrims.

steps.title: The butter thief
steps.text: Krishna and Balarama grow up among the cowherds. Krishna steals butter from the neighbours’ pots and shares it with the monkeys. The women complain to Yashoda. When the boys report that he has eaten earth, Yashoda makes him open his mouth and sees the whole universe inside. Then he lets her forget, and she is simply his mother again.
steps.today: The butter thief (makhan chor) is one of the best-loved images of Krishna in temples and in Braj Bhasha poetry.

steps.title: Tied to the mortar
steps.text: Yashoda tries to tie him to a wooden mortar, but every rope is two fingers short until he lets himself be bound. Dragging the mortar between twin arjuna trees, he pulls them down, freeing two sons of Kubera whom the sage Narada had cursed to stand as trees. He is called Damodara, ‘rope round the belly’.
steps.today: Many devotees keep the autumn month of Kartika as Damodara month, singing a hymn to the bound child.

steps.title: The move to Vrindavan
steps.text: Alarmed by these portents, the cowherds load their carts and move to the forest of Vrindavan, beside the Yamuna and Govardhan hill. The boys herd the calves, then the cows. Demons keep coming: a giant crane, a python whose open mouth the boys mistake for a cave, an ass demon in a palm grove whom Balarama kills.
steps.today: Vrindavan, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, a town of thousands of temples.

steps.title: Kaliya’s pool
steps.text: The many-headed serpent Kaliya poisons a pool of the Yamuna so that birds flying over it fall dead. Krishna climbs a kadamba tree, leaps into the water and lets the serpent coil around him, then dances on its hoods until it vomits blood. Kaliya’s wives plead for him, and Krishna sends him away to the sea.
steps.today: Kaliya Ghat in Vrindavan is shown as the pool, beside a kadamba tree.

steps.title: Lifting Govardhan
steps.text: Krishna persuades the cowherds to honour their hill, their cows and the Brahmins instead of holding their yearly offering to Indra, god of rain. Indra, furious, sends a storm that lasts seven days. Krishna lifts Govardhan hill on one hand like an umbrella, and all Vraja shelters beneath it. Indra yields, and Krishna is named Govinda.
steps.today: Pilgrims walk the 21-kilometre path around Govardhan hill. Govardhan Puja and the ‘mountain of food’ (Annakut), the day after Diwali, recall it.

steps.title: The dance on the autumn night
steps.text: On a full-moon night in autumn, Krishna plays his flute and the cowherd women (gopis) leave their homes to join him in the forest. When they grow proud, he vanishes with one of them, then leaves her too. They search for him, singing. He returns and, in the circle dance (rasa), multiplies so that each dancer has him beside her.
steps.today: Nidhivan and Seva Kunj, groves in Vrindavan, are honoured as sites of the dance. The Bhagavata’s five chapters on it are among its most read.

steps.title: Radha
steps.text: The Bhagavata does not name the gopi Krishna favours. Later tradition does: Radha. She appears in early Prakrit verse, then becomes the heart of Jayadeva’s twelfth-century Gita Govinda and of Vrindavan’s devotion, where she is worshipped with Krishna as one. Tradition makes her the daughter of Vrishabhanu of Barsana.
steps.today: Barsana, about 45 kilometres north-west of Mathura, honours Radha. At its Holi, women of Barsana drive off the men of Nandgaon with sticks.

steps.title: Akrura’s chariot
steps.text: Kamsa sends Akrura, a Yadava elder, to bring the brothers to a festival of the bow, meaning to kill them there. The gopis beg the chariot to stop. Bathing in the Yamuna on the way, Akrura sees Krishna and Balarama in the water, then Vishnu lying on the serpent Shesha. Krishna never returns to Vraja.
steps.today: Akrur Ghat, between Vrindavan and Mathura, is shown as the place of Akrura’s vision.

steps.title: The end of Kamsa
steps.text: In Mathura, Krishna straightens the back of a hunchbacked woman, Trivakra, and breaks the great bow. Next morning he kills the elephant Kuvalayapida at the arena gate, and the brothers kill the champion wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika. Krishna leaps onto Kamsa’s dais, drags him down and kills him. Ugrasena is crowned again; Devaki and Vasudeva are freed.
steps.today: Vishram Ghat, Mathura, where tradition says Krishna rested after killing Kamsa, holds the evening river worship (aarti).

steps.title: The teacher at Avanti
steps.text: The brothers study with the sage Sandipani at Avanti (Ujjain), learning the sixty-four arts in sixty-four days; a poor Brahmin pupil becomes Krishna’s friend. As his fee, Sandipani asks for his son, drowned at Prabhasa. Krishna kills the sea demon Panchajana, takes his conch, Panchajanya, and brings the boy back from Yama, god of death.
steps.today: Sandipani Ashram at Ankapat, Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, is honoured as the school.

steps.title: The song of the bee
steps.text: Krishna sends his friend Uddhava, a learned counsellor, to console Nanda, Yashoda and the gopis and teach them that Krishna is everywhere. One gopi speaks to a passing bee as if it were Krishna’s messenger, scolding the fickle lover. Uddhava is humbled: their longing, he decides, is the highest devotion.
steps.today: The Song of the Bee (Bhramara Gita) inspired centuries of poems in Braj Bhasha, notably by Surdas.

steps.title: Seventeen sieges
steps.text: Kamsa’s two widows are daughters of Jarasandha, king of Magadha. He marches on Mathura seventeen times and is beaten back every time. Before the eighteenth attack, a foreign king, Kalayavana, besieges the city too. Krishna lures him into a cave, where the sleeping king Muchukunda, woken by a kick, burns him to ashes with a glance.
steps.today: Machkund, near Dholpur, Rajasthan, is one site claimed for Muchukunda’s cave.

steps.title: A city in the sea
steps.text: Krishna has the divine builder Vishvakarma raise a fortress city in the sea, Dwaraka, and moves the Yadavas there overnight. In the Mahabharata, Krishna tells it plainly: the Yadavas left Mathura for fear of Jarasandha and settled at Kushasthali, by Mount Raivataka. Krishna and Balarama, fleeing Jarasandha on foot, give him the slip.
steps.today: Dwarka, Gujarat. As ‘he who left the battlefield’ (Ranchhodrai), Krishna is worshipped at Dwarka and Dakor.

steps.title: Rukmini’s letter
steps.text: Princess Rukmini of Vidarbha loves Krishna, but her brother Rukmi has promised her to King Shishupala of Chedi. She sends a Brahmin to Dwaraka with a letter asking Krishna to carry her off. He takes her in his chariot as she leaves the goddess’s temple, beats the pursuing kings, and spares Rukmi at her plea, shaving his head in patches.
steps.today: Kaundinyapur on the Wardha river, Amravati district, Maharashtra, is honoured as Kundina. Madhavpur, on the Gujarat coast, celebrates the wedding at a spring fair.

steps.title: The Syamantaka jewel
steps.text: The Sun gives Satrajit a jewel, Syamantaka. His brother wears it hunting and is killed by a lion, the lion by Jambavan, king of the bears. Accused of theft, Krishna tracks it to Jambavan’s cave and fights him for twenty-eight days. Jambavan, knowing Rama in him, yields the jewel and his daughter Jambavati. Satrajit, ashamed, gives Krishna his daughter Satyabhama.
steps.today: A cave at Ranavav, near Porbandar, Gujarat, is one site claimed as Jambavan’s.

steps.title: Naraka
steps.text: Naraka, son of the Earth and king of Pragjyotisha, steals the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and holds 16,100 princesses captive. Krishna flies there on Garuda with Satyabhama. He kills the five-headed demon Mura, earning the name Murari, and then Naraka. He marries the freed women, and carries off the Parijata tree from Indra’s heaven.
steps.today: Guwahati, Assam, is honoured as Pragjyotisha. In much of India, Naraka Chaturdashi, the day before Diwali, marks his defeat.

steps.title: Usha’s dream
steps.text: Usha, daughter of the thousand-armed Bana, dreams of a young man. Her friend Chitralekha paints portraits until Usha knows him, Krishna’s grandson Aniruddha, then carries him from Dwaraka by magic. Bana imprisons him. Krishna attacks Shonitapura, battles Bana’s protector, Shiva himself, and cuts off all but four of Bana’s arms. Usha and Aniruddha marry.
steps.today: Tezpur, Assam, is honoured as Shonitapura, with Agnigarh hill as Usha’s fort. Ukhimath, Uttarakhand, also claims the couple’s wedding.

steps.title: A handful of flattened rice
steps.text: Krishna’s poor schoolfriend from Avanti comes to Dwaraka with nothing to give but a handful of flattened rice, tied in a rag. Krishna washes his feet and eats the rice with delight. The friend asks for nothing, and goes home to find his hut turned into a mansion. The Bhagavata does not name him; later tradition calls him Sudama.
steps.today: Porbandar’s Sudama temple honours the town as his home. In Kerala he is Kuchela, remembered at Guruvayur each December.

steps.title: Arjuna and Subhadra
steps.text: The five Pandava brothers are Krishna’s cousins, sons of his father’s sister Kunti. When Arjuna, on a pilgrimage, falls in love with Krishna’s sister Subhadra at a festival on Mount Raivataka, Krishna advises him to carry her off. Balarama is furious until Krishna calms him. Their son, Abhimanyu, will die at Kurukshetra.
steps.today: Girnar, near Junagadh, Gujarat, is usually identified as Mount Raivataka.

steps.title: The Khandava forest
steps.text: Krishna and Arjuna help the fire god Agni burn the Khandava forest, holding off Indra’s rain. Krishna receives his discus, Sudarshana, and his mace; Arjuna receives the bow Gandiva. Among the few spared is the demon architect Maya, who in thanks builds the Pandavas a marvellous assembly hall at Indraprastha.
steps.today: Delhi’s Purana Qila is the traditional site of Indraprastha.

steps.title: Jarasandha’s end
steps.text: Yudhishthira wants to hold a royal consecration, but Jarasandha holds eighty-six kings captive for a sacrifice. Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna enter Girivraja dressed as Brahmins and challenge him to single combat. Bhima wrestles him for days on end and kills him. The captive kings go free, and Jarasandha’s son Sahadeva rules Magadha as an ally.
steps.today: Jarasandh ka Akhara, Rajgir, Bihar, is shown as the wrestling ground.

steps.title: Shishupala
steps.text: At Yudhishthira’s consecration, Bhishma names Krishna the guest of honour. Shishupala of Chedi, Rukmini’s jilted suitor, heaps insults on him. Krishna had promised Shishupala’s mother, his aunt, to forgive her son a hundred offences. When the hundredth is passed, he cuts off Shishupala’s head with his discus.
steps.today: Chedi lay in Bundelkhand, central India.

steps.title: The peace mission
steps.text: After the Pandavas’ thirteen years of exile, Krishna drives to Hastinapura to make peace. Duryodhana will not give them as much land as a needle’s point covers, and plots to seize Krishna. Krishna shows the court his universal form, filled with gods, then leaves. Before going, he tells Karna that he is Kunti’s eldest son.
steps.today: Hastinapur, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: The Song of the Lord
steps.text: At Kurukshetra, Arjuna, with Krishna as his unarmed charioteer, sees his teachers and kin in the enemy ranks and lays down his bow. Krishna’s answer is the Bhagavad Gita: act from duty, without attachment to the results, and offer every act to God. He shows Arjuna his universal form, the source and end of all things.
steps.today: Jyotisar, Kurukshetra, Haryana, with its banyan tree, is honoured as the place of the Gita.

steps.title: The charioteer’s war
steps.text: Krishna has sworn not to fight. Twice, when Bhishma presses Arjuna hard, he leaps down to attack Bhishma on foot. His advice turns the war: kill an elephant named Ashvatthama so Drona believes his son is dead; strike Karna while his wheel is stuck; break Duryodhana’s thigh. The epic does not hide that victory comes through ruses.
steps.today: As Arjuna’s charioteer, Krishna is worshipped as Parthasarathy, notably at Thiruvallikeni, Chennai.

steps.title: Gandhari’s curse
steps.text: Walking the battlefield among the dead, Gandhari, mother of the hundred Kauravas, blames Krishna, who could have stopped the war. She curses him: in thirty-six years his own clan will kill one another, and he will die alone in the forest. Krishna accepts it calmly; he had already foreseen the Yadavas’ end.
steps.today: The Mahabharata’s eleventh book, the Book of the Women (Stri Parva), tells it.

steps.title: The iron club
steps.text: Young Yadavas dress Krishna’s son Samba as a pregnant woman and ask visiting sages what she will bear. The sages curse them: an iron club that will destroy the clan. Samba gives birth to one. King Ugrasena has it ground to powder and thrown into the sea, where it washes up as reeds. A fish swallows the last lump.
steps.today: The Bhagavata sets the curse at Pindaraka; Pindara, on the coast east of Dwarka, is identified with it.

steps.title: The last teaching
steps.text: As ill omens multiply, Uddhava begs to go with Krishna. Krishna gives him instead a long final teaching on detachment, devotion and seeing God in all beings: the Uddhava Gita, in the Bhagavata’s eleventh book. Then he sends Uddhava to the hermitage at Badari in the Himalaya, and leads the Yadavas to Prabhasa.
steps.today: Badrinath, Uttarakhand, is the Badari of tradition.

steps.title: The hunter’s arrow
steps.text: At Prabhasa the drunken Yadavas quarrel and kill one another with the reeds, which turn to clubs. Balarama gives up his life by the sea. Krishna rests beneath a tree; a hunter, Jara,, taking his foot for a deer, shoots it with an arrow tipped from the last iron lump. Krishna forgives him and leaves the world.
steps.today: Bhalka Tirtha, near Somnath, Gujarat, is shown as the place. Indian astronomers counted the present age (Kali Yuga), which tradition says began as Krishna left, from 3102 BCE.

steps.title: The sea takes Dwaraka
steps.text: Krishna’s charioteer Daruka carries the news to Arjuna. Arjuna leads the women and survivors out, and behind them the sea floods Dwaraka. He installs Krishna’s great-grandson Vajra as king: at Indraprastha in the Mahabharata, at Mathura in the Bhagavata. The Pandavas, their purpose gone, soon set out on their last journey.
steps.today: Tradition credits Vajra with the first shrines at Mathura and Dwarka. Underwater surveys off Dwarka found stone structures whose age is debated.

steps.title: Vasudeva, god of gods
steps.text: Krishna appears early in the record. The Chandogya Upanishad names a Krishna, son of Devaki, and the grammarian Panini mentions devotion to Vasudeva. About 300 BCE, Megasthenes wrote of a Heracles honoured around Methora, which many scholars read as Krishna at Mathura. At Vidisha, a Greek envoy, Heliodorus, raised a pillar to ‘Vasudeva, god of gods’.
steps.today: The Heliodorus pillar stands at Besnagar, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: The Gita Govinda
steps.text: The poet Jayadeva writes the Gita Govinda, a Sanskrit song cycle on the longing, quarrel and reunion of Radha and Krishna in the spring forest. Sung in the Jagannath temple at Puri and danced in Odissi, it set the mood of later devotion. Jayadeva’s birthplace is claimed by both Kenduli in Bengal and Kenduli Sasan in Odisha.
steps.today: Puri, Odisha. The Gita Govinda is still sung in the Jagannath temple’s rituals.

steps.title: Vrindavan rediscovered
steps.text: By the 1500s, followers say, many of Vraja’s sacred sites were forgotten. The Bengali saint Chaitanya visited about 1515 and sent disciples, the Goswamis, who settled at Vrindavan, identified the sites and wrote its theology. Vallabhacharya founded worship at Govardhan. In 1590 Raja Man Singh of Amber built Vrindavan’s great Govinda Dev temple, which still stands.
steps.today: Most of Vraja’s shrines date from the 16th century onwards. ISKCON, founded in New York in 1966, carried this devotion worldwide.

items.name: Vasudeva
items.text: A Yadava of the Vrishni clan, and brother of Kunti, mother of the Pandavas. Bound by his promise, he hands Kamsa six of his sons, then carries the eighth across the Yamuna to safety. Of his wives, Rohini, Balarama’s mother, lives in Gokula. In the Mahabharata he dies at Dwaraka, grieving for Krishna.

items.name: Devaki
items.text: Daughter of Devaka, and so Kamsa’s cousin, though retellings often call her his sister. She spends years in his prison and loses six sons to him. Krishna, her eighth child, frees her only when he is grown. A late chapter of the Bhagavata has him bring back her six dead sons for her to see.

items.name: Yashoda
items.text: Wife of Nanda, in Gokula and Vrindavan. Her own newborn daughter is the baby swapped for Krishna. Devotional poetry dwells on her: chasing the butter thief, tying him to the mortar, seeing the universe in his mouth. Her love for the child is the model of a parent’s devotion (vatsalya).

items.name: Nanda
items.text: Chief of the cowherds of Gokula and a friend of Vasudeva. He leads the move to Vrindavan and, at Krishna’s urging, honours Govardhan instead of Indra. When Krishna stays in Mathura, Nanda goes home without him. Nandgaon, a hilltop village near Barsana, is honoured as his home.

items.name: Balarama
items.text: Son of Vasudeva and Rohini, drawn from Devaki’s womb before birth, hence his name Sankarshana. Strong and hot-tempered, he carries a plough and a club. He teaches both Bhima and Duryodhana the club and stays out of the war, on pilgrimage. Tradition counts him a form of the serpent Shesha; some lists make him an avatar of Vishnu.

items.name: Kamsa
items.text: Son of Ugrasena, whom he deposes. Married to two daughters of Jarasandha, he has a powerful ally. Warned that Devaki’s eighth child will kill him, he kills her children, sends demons after the infant Krishna, then lures him to Mathura to be killed. Krishna kills him there instead.

items.name: Radha
items.text: The gopi most loved by Krishna in later tradition, though the Bhagavata, Vishnu Purana and Harivamsha do not name her. Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda makes her its heroine, and Bengal’s Vaishnavas and the Vrindavan schools worship her as Krishna’s own joy and power. Tradition makes her the daughter of Vrishabhanu and Kirti of Barsana.

items.name: Akrura
items.text: A Yadava elder at Kamsa’s court and, in secret, Krishna’s devotee. Sent to fetch the brothers to their deaths, he is shown Vishnu in the Yamuna on the way. His name means ‘not cruel’, though the gopis call him cruel for taking Krishna away. In the Syamantaka story the jewel ends up in his keeping.

items.name: Uddhava
items.text: A Yadava, Krishna’s cousin and closest counsellor, a pupil of Brihaspati, teacher of the gods. Sent to console the gopis, he goes to teach and comes back taught. Before the end, Krishna gives him his last teaching, the Uddhava Gita, and sends him to Badari to carry it on.

items.name: Jarasandha
items.text: King of Magadha, ruling from Girivraja. Born in two halves, he was joined into one by a demoness named Jara, hence his name. Kamsa’s father-in-law, he attacks Mathura again and again, drives the Yadavas west and gathers captive kings for a sacrifice, until Bhima kills him in single combat.

items.name: Rukmini
items.text: Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhishmaka. Her seven-verse letter to Krishna is one of the Bhagavata’s best-loved passages. Mother of Pradyumna, and so grandmother of Aniruddha. Worshipped as a form of Lakshmi, she is honoured beside Vithoba at Pandharpur, Maharashtra, as Rakhumai.

items.name: Satyabhama
items.text: Daughter of Satrajit, given to Krishna after the Syamantaka affair. Proud and spirited, she rides Garuda with him to fight Naraka, and it is for her that he carries off the Parijata tree from Indra’s heaven. Some popular tellings, especially in the south, make her the one who kills Naraka.

items.name: Sudama
items.text: Krishna’s poor Brahmin friend from their schooldays with Sandipani. The Bhagavata calls him only a Brahmin friend; later tradition names him Sudama, and in the south Kuchela, ‘poorly clothed’. His handful of flattened rice is told as the model of love given without asking anything back.

items.name: Arjuna
items.text: Third of the Pandava brothers, son of Kunti, and husband of Krishna’s sister Subhadra. The epic calls the two friends Nara and Narayana, ancient sages reborn. Krishna drives his chariot through the war and speaks the Gita to him. After Krishna’s death, Arjuna’s strength fails him on the road from Dwaraka.
